steps.title: Key Context
steps.body: After Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570, Catholic plots to overthrow her intensified. Mary Queen of Scots, Elizabeth's Catholic cousin, was the focal point of every conspiracy - she was the obvious Catholic alternative to Elizabeth. Elizabeth's survival depended on her spy network, led by Francis Walsingham, and her ability to outmanoeuvre the plotters without provoking an international crisis.

steps.title: Significance of the Revolt
steps.body: The Revolt of the Northern Earls was the only armed Catholic uprising of Elizabeth's reign. It showed that Catholic nobles in the north were willing to use force, but it also demonstrated the limits of their support. Most ordinary people, even Catholics, were unwilling to risk their lives for the cause. The revolt's failure strengthened Elizabeth's position and led to harsher measures against Catholics.

steps.title: Walsingham's Spy Network
steps.body: The Ridolfi Plot was discovered through the intelligence network of Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth's "spymaster." Walsingham (1532-1590) built an extensive network of agents and informers across England and Europe. He intercepted letters, employed double agents, and used codes and ciphers to gather intelligence. His network was so effective that he often knew of Catholic plots before they were fully formed. Walsingham's espionage was crucial to Elizabeth's survival throughout her reign.

steps.title: Phelippes' Forgery
steps.body: When Thomas Phelippes decoded Mary's letter of 17 July 1586, he added a postscript in Mary's cipher requesting the names of the conspirators. This was designed to extract more evidence, but the conspirators were arrested before they could respond. The fact that Walsingham's team forged part of the letter has led some historians to question whether the evidence was entirely fair - but Mary's approval of the assassination plot was genuinely in her own hand.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know all four plots in chronological order: 1569, 1571, 1583, 1586 Always use specific dates and named individuals Explain Walsingham's methods in detail - the Babington Plot trap is a very common question For comparison questions, structure around similarities AND differences Link the plots together - show how they escalated and how Elizabeth's response intensified Remember the significance of Mary's execution: it removed the threat but provoked the Armada For evaluation questions, balance the danger of the plots against their failure
